ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: We primarily hypothesised that whilst multisensory stimulation is the most important factor in the creation of presence, unisensory touch will be a greater causative factor in the creation of presence than unisensory vision. 44 participants completed an implicit reaction-time task (reacting to target stimuli) and an explicit metacognitive task (rating confidence in object presence).

Participants were automatically excluded from participating further in the study if they answered TRUE when asked if they had experienced a history of motion sickness in the demographics questionnaire.
No participants were excluded. 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male) were therefore recruited through the UCL SONA system.
Participants were aged 18 or above and provided informed consent before taking part in the study.

Age was included as people's reaction times tend to increase with age, and VR and VR haptics familiarity scores (how familiar participants were with VR and VR haptic technology on a scale of 0-5) were included as controls as participants with more experience in VR would feasibly do 'better' in both tasks than participants who were not as familiar with VR and had to learn the technology as they completed the task.
table.header: Figure 1 Graphical Display of Conditions Note.

table.text: In total, we recruited and tested 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male).
In the VR environment, participants are sat in the centre of a steel minecart travelling slowly along tracks within this cave system.
Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure 2).
table.formatted: Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

table.text: Stimulus 1 is the target stimulus participants were trained on.
In this block, participants were told that the target stimuli they had been trained on was a species of Bat which was dangerous to humans.
Participants were tasked to remove the Bat from the cave by activating an inbuilt laser system by pressing the left index trigger on the left controller.
Participants were updated on how many laser activations they had remaining through a number shown to them in the VR headset.
Participants were also given a health bar which acted as an incentive for them to perform as well as possible during the task.
Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted.

Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block.

In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure 5 for a summary of key differences).
table.formatted: In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">5</ref> for a summary of key differences).

table.text: Participants gave their answers on a confidence scale from 0-100, with 0 indicating a strong confidence that the stimulus just presented to them was the target stimulus, and 100 indicating that the stimulus just presented to them was not the target stimulus.

In the confidence block, participants were asked to rate each stimulus following stimulus presentation, whereas in the reaction time block participants were asked to react by pressing a button if they thought they experienced the target stimulus.
Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted.

Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block.

Analysis 3b -We will determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.
Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value.
We also aimed to determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials.

After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table 4).
table.formatted: After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

table.text: We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001).
table.formatted: We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001).

table.text: Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value.

We found that participants were significantly less accurate in multisensory scenarios in which vision appeared before touch than in scenarios where touch appeared before vision (𝜷 = -.037, SE = .011, t(297.93) = -3.32, p = .001**).
Participants were asked how real each modality felt.
This study found that, although participants had some limited global, task-level insight into their performance, this was uncorrelated with the triallevel insight measured during the task.

Our finding that participants were faster in multisensory scenarios compared to unisensory scenarios suggests that, despite the novelty of mid-air haptics, multisensory mechanisms were still recruited when participants were presented with a visual stimulus accompanied by a haptic stimulus produced via novel mid-air haptics.
Our results also show that participants were faster at responding to the presence of target objects in unisensory vision trials compared to unisensory touch trials.

Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception (Fan et al., 2020; Mayeli, 2019; Stokes & Biggs, 2014) by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision.
table.formatted: Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mayeli, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stokes & Biggs, 2014)</ref> by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision.

table.text: This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms (Gomez et al., 2018; Snow & Culham, 2021).
table.formatted: This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gomez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Snow & Culham, 2021)</ref>.

table.text: Although we found no difference in metacognitive ability between unisensory touch and unisensory visual trials in our confidence block, exploratory analysis 3b did find that participants were significantly more accurate in unisensory touch trials compared to unisensory visual trials.
However, we also found that participants were more accurate in multisensory conditions where touch was presented before vision than conditions in which vision was presented before touch.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample size estimation was based on a power analysis performed on hypothesis 1 using G*Power3.1 (Faul et al., 2007). For our study, with Multisensory Order and Unisensory Modality (not their interaction) as our two main independent variables of interest regarding hypothesis 1, a moderate effect size of .4 (Barutchu & Spence, 2021), a power of .8, and alpha of .05, the recommended total sample size is 40 participants. The moderate effect size utilised in this power calculation was based on a behavioural sensory-switching study undertaken by Barutchu & Spence (2021), since the core dependent variable (reaction time) and independent variables remain consistent with our study. In total, we recruited and tested 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 866 columns across 139 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Presence Questionnaire.csv", "Presence Questionnaire.csv", "Presence Questionnaire.csv", "SART_Master.csv", "VDTMasterData.csv" ), Column = c("Q11", "Q12", "Q13", "Go/NoGo", "Trial No."), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 63 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: no/No/NO", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: n/a/N/A", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"/\")", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"p\"" )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Qualtrics Survey Metadata

2 of the 139 data files are a Qualtrics survey export. The table below summarises the response metadata Qualtrics records for every survey (not the substantive question columns): how many rows look like previews or unfinished responses that usually need dropping before analysis, the typical completion time (with a count of implausibly fast responses), the data-collection window, and which Qualtrics fields carry personal information to review before sharing.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Presence Questionnaire.csv", "Bat Experiment Survey.csv"
), Responses = c(44L, 44L), "Preview/unfinished" = c(0L, 0L), 
    "Median time" = c("4.0 min", "1.8 min"), "Very fast" = c("2", 
    "7"), Collected = c("—", "—"), "PII fields" = c("none", 
    "none")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```
#### Careless Responding
No respondent was flagged for straightlining in the 1 file that could be screened.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 139 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We primarily hypothesised that whilst multisensory stimulation is the most important factor in the creation of presence, unisensory touch will be a greater causative factor in the creation of presence than unisensory vision. 44 participants completed an implicit reaction-time task (reacting to target stimuli) and an explicit metacognitive task (rating confidence in object presence).

Participants were automatically excluded from participating further in the study if they answered TRUE when asked if they had experienced a history of motion sickness in the demographics questionnaire.
No participants were excluded. 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male) were therefore recruited through the UCL SONA system.
Participants were aged 18 or above and provided informed consent before taking part in the study.

Age was included as people's reaction times tend to increase with age, and VR and VR haptics familiarity scores (how familiar participants were with VR and VR haptic technology on a scale of 0-5) were included as controls as participants with more experience in VR would feasibly do 'better' in both tasks than participants who were not as familiar with VR and had to learn the technology as they completed the task.
In total, we recruited and tested 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male).
In the VR environment, participants are sat in the centre of a steel minecart travelling slowly along tracks within this cave system.
Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure 2).
Stimulus 1 is the target stimulus participants were trained on.
In this block, participants were told that the target stimuli they had been trained on was a species of Bat which was dangerous to humans.
Participants were tasked to remove the Bat from the cave by activating an inbuilt laser system by pressing the left index trigger on the left controller.
Participants were updated on how many laser activations they had remaining through a number shown to them in the VR headset.
Participants were also given a health bar which acted as an incentive for them to perform as well as possible during the task.
Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted.

Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block.

In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure 5 for a summary of key differences).

Participants gave their answers on a confidence scale from 0-100, with 0 indicating a strong confidence that the stimulus just presented to them was the target stimulus, and 100 indicating that the stimulus just presented to them was not the target stimulus.

In the confidence block, participants were asked to rate each stimulus following stimulus presentation, whereas in the reaction time block participants were asked to react by pressing a button if they thought they experienced the target stimulus.

Analysis 3b -We will determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.
Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value.
We also aimed to determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials.

After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table 4).
We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001).

We found that participants were significantly less accurate in multisensory scenarios in which vision appeared before touch than in scenarios where touch appeared before vision (𝜷 = -.037, SE = .011, t(297.93) = -3.32, p = .001**).
Participants were asked how real each modality felt.
This study found that, although participants had some limited global, task-level insight into their performance, this was uncorrelated with the triallevel insight measured during the task.

Our finding that participants were faster in multisensory scenarios compared to unisensory scenarios suggests that, despite the novelty of mid-air haptics, multisensory mechanisms were still recruited when participants were presented with a visual stimulus accompanied by a haptic stimulus produced via novel mid-air haptics.
Our results also show that participants were faster at responding to the presence of target objects in unisensory vision trials compared to unisensory touch trials.

Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception (Fan et al., 2020; Mayeli, 2019; Stokes & Biggs, 2014) by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision.

This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms (Gomez et al., 2018; Snow & Culham, 2021).

Although we found no difference in metacognitive ability between unisensory touch and unisensory visual trials in our confidence block, exploratory analysis 3b did find that participants were significantly more accurate in unisensory touch trials compared to unisensory visual trials.
However, we also found that participants were more accurate in multisensory conditions where touch was presented before vision than conditions in which vision was presented before touch.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "BatExpAnalysis (2).R", "Runs after" = "—", 
    Basis = "numeric"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `mratioresults23.csv`, `mratioresults45.csv`.
#### Execution

info.title: Identifying Discrepancies Between Measurements of Visual, Felt Presence and Tactile, Judged Presence

author.affiliation:
Clinical, Educational & Health Psychology Research Department
								Division of Psychology & Language Sciences
								University College London

text.text: Unlike other screen-based technologies such as computer monitors, virtual reality (VR) systems allow the user to feel a sense of presence -the sense that they are actually situated within the surrounding virtual environment.

Although the foundational experience of existing within a physical environment goes far beyond aspects of vision, our study is the first, to our knowledge, to operationalise and measure different facets of the multidimensional concept of the SOOP, ranging from indirect, trial-by-trial measures of reaction times and accuracy to higher-order aspects of presence judgements such as their trial-by-trial metacognitive efficiency, and to modality-specific and modality-general global (i.e. across many trials), retrospective self-report measures.

We primarily hypothesised that whilst multisensory stimulation is the most important factor in the creation of presence, unisensory touch will be a greater causative factor in the creation of presence than unisensory vision. 44 participants completed an implicit reaction-time task (reacting to target stimuli) and an explicit metacognitive task (rating confidence in object presence).
We manipulated sense type (unisensory vs multisensory), sensory modality (vision vs touch) and temporal order (e.g., touch-first vs. vision-first).
Results indicated that multisensory integration significantly enhanced metacognitive efficacy, accuracy and reaction speeds compared to unisensory conditions.
However, a key dissociation emerged between unisensory modalities.

While participants reacted faster to visual stimuli, they achieved higher perceptual accuracy with tactile stimuli, with participants retrospectively rating touch as feeling significantly more "real" than vision.
These findings support the notion that realtime "felt" presence and retrospective "judged" presence may be caused by distinct factors.

In both cognitive science and VR research, the sense of presence (SOP) is defined as the feeling of existing within one's surrounding environment (Metzinger, 2003; Sanchez-Vives & Slater, 2005; Singleton & Fotopoulou, 2026).
text.formatted: In both cognitive science and VR research, the sense of presence (SOP) is defined as the feeling of existing within one's surrounding environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Metzinger, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Sanchez-Vives & Slater, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Singleton & Fotopoulou, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While the technological and cognitive determinants of SOP, such as field-of-view, latency, and agency are well-documented (e.g., Hendrix & Barfield, 1996; Nakano et al., 2021; Slater, 2009), less is known about how we perceive the presence of inanimate objects, hereafter referred to as the 'Sense of Object Presence' (SOOP).
text.formatted: While the technological and cognitive determinants of SOP, such as field-of-view, latency, and agency are well-documented (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hendrix & Barfield, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Nakano et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Slater, 2009)</ref>, less is known about how we perceive the presence of inanimate objects, hereafter referred to as the 'Sense of Object Presence' (SOOP).

text.text: Specifically, the role of proximal senses, such as touch, remains underexplored compared to visual dominance.
For the purposes of the current study, we specifically relate our hypotheses, analyses and discussion to the SOOP rather than the SOP.
This is not because we see the SOOP as a distinct concept from the SOP (SOOP would be a subset of SOP (Seth, 2014)) -instead the reasons for this are entirely driven by experimental pragmatics.
text.formatted: This is not because we see the SOOP as a distinct concept from the SOP (SOOP would be a subset of SOP <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Seth, 2014)</ref>) -instead the reasons for this are entirely driven by experimental pragmatics.

text.text: Usually in presence research, the dependent variables (normally measures of how present one feels in the virtual environment) relate to the entire virtual environment as a whole rather than any specific subset of that environment (Suzuki et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Usually in presence research, the dependent variables (normally measures of how present one feels in the virtual environment) relate to the entire virtual environment as a whole rather than any specific subset of that environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Suzuki et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Even when studies manipulate one specific aspect of the environment (such as gravity, embodiment, etc. (Drori et al., 2025)), the dependent variables collected relate to a participant's entire experience rather than the specific manipulation.
text.formatted: Even when studies manipulate one specific aspect of the environment (such as gravity, embodiment, etc. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Drori et al., 2025)</ref>), the dependent variables collected relate to a participant's entire experience rather than the specific manipulation.

text.text: However, in the current study our dependent variables relate to the specific manipulation of how participants interact with objects, in that we attempt to determine whether participants feel as if the objects presented to them are also present in the virtual space with them.

Augmented reality (AR) paradigms may also be suited to answer this type of question, though there may be a potential mismatch in that an AR paradigm would be asking participants whether they felt as if a virtual object was present in the physical world, whereas our VR paradigm asks whether this virtual object feels present within the virtual world.

Therefore, due to this specific difference between the current study and previous studies, and for the sake of precision and transparency, we will instead conduct and discuss our experiment with reference to object presence (SOOP) than general presence, despite the fact that the SOOP is merely a more specific instance of the SOP (Suzuki et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Therefore, due to this specific difference between the current study and previous studies, and for the sake of precision and transparency, we will instead conduct and discuss our experiment with reference to object presence (SOOP) than general presence, despite the fact that the SOOP is merely a more specific instance of the SOP <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Suzuki et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Most previous research on the SOP and SOOP has focused on the role of distant sensory modalities such as vision, or audition, with only limited research examining proximal sensations such as touch.
Touch is considered a proximal modality in the sense that to touch an object or be touched by it, that object needs to be near to the body.
The current emphasis on distant modalities may have been due to the ease by which one can present or manipulate visual and auditory stimuli in related experimental paradigms and VR settings.

However, such differences in research volume could introduce an unintentional bias in the understanding of the SOOP, potentially underestimating the specific role of proximal sensory modalities, such as touch.
This specificity may, for example, stem from the fact that typically, we will first see or hear an approaching object, and we will only be able to touch it when we are near it.
In other terms, touch of an object is habitually added to its multisensory perception later than distant modalities such as vision.

Moreover, perceiving an object near the body (in its so-called peripersonal space) is known to recruit different neural and perceptual processes than perceiving an object far from the body, both because proximity allows for action towards the world and because the body needs to be defended from potential threats in the environment (Serino, 2019 (Serino, , 2022)).
text.formatted: Moreover, perceiving an object near the body (in its so-called peripersonal space) is known to recruit different neural and perceptual processes than perceiving an object far from the body, both because proximity allows for action towards the world and because the body needs to be defended from potential threats in the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Serino, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Serino, , 2022))</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, the effects of this proximity and habitual temporal order by which we perceive objects to the sense of presence have not been examined.
According to some philosophers, touch can be a 'reality verificator' (Massin, 2009; Merleau-Ponty, 2002).
text.formatted: According to some philosophers, touch can be a 'reality verificator' <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Massin, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Merleau-Ponty, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is unclear as to whether this is because touch is typically the last modality used to verify the perceptual content of other modalities, or whether there is something intrinsically different about the information touch adds to the SOOP.
Indeed, touch does display some other unique properties.

For example, we cannot touch an object without being touched back; a reciprocal relationship between body and objects that has led some philosophers to claim that touch has a unique role in a related concept, the sense of reality (SOR) -one's subjective sense of reality of the world and the self positioned within it (Metzinger, 2003; (Merleau-Ponty, 2002)  (Massin, 2009).
text.formatted: For example, we cannot touch an object without being touched back; a reciprocal relationship between body and objects that has led some philosophers to claim that touch has a unique role in a related concept, the sense of reality (SOR) -one's subjective sense of reality of the world and the self positioned within it <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Metzinger, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Merleau-Ponty, 2002)</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Massin, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Only four studies have directly compared touch to other unisensory or multisensory stimuli in creating the sense of presence in VR.
Two of these studies found that the addition of touch feedback to vision increased self-reported presence (Brasen et al., 2019; Kreimeier et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Two of these studies found that the addition of touch feedback to vision increased self-reported presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brasen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kreimeier et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, both studies utilised a relatively small sample size (N =14 in both), indicating a low power for the intended effect size.
A third study found that the addition of touch feedback directly to the hands during a game of Simon Says did not increase presence (Viciana-Abad et al., 2010).
text.formatted: A third study found that the addition of touch feedback directly to the hands during a game of Simon Says did not increase presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Viciana-Abad et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, presence was only increased when participants utilised a stylus to press the virtual buttons, receiving touch feedback via the stylus (Viciana-Abad et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Rather, presence was only increased when participants utilised a stylus to press the virtual buttons, receiving touch feedback via the stylus <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Viciana-Abad et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A final study not only found that the addition of touch feedback to visual events in VR enhanced presence, but that touch feedback alone seemed to contribute more to presence than visual feedback alone (Gibbs et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A final study not only found that the addition of touch feedback to visual events in VR enhanced presence, but that touch feedback alone seemed to contribute more to presence than visual feedback alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gibbs et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, this was the first study to conduct such direct, unisensory comparisons between touch and vision.
Collectively, these four studies suggest that the addition of touch, or at least certain types of touch, to multisensory VR experiences can enhance self-reported SOP.
However, strong conclusions cannot be made from these such varied and small sample studies that relied only on self-report.

The current, well-powered study aimed to compare directly between touch and vision in both unisensory and multisensory conditions, as well as to utilise indirect (reaction times) and trial-by-trial (visual analogue scale (VAS) ratings) behavioural and metacognitive measures of the SOOP to provide greater reliability and specificity to our understanding of the role of touch in SOOP.

Moreover, we are also interested in how the order of stimulus presentation within a multisensory context impacts the SOOP, given the aforementioned 'proximal' properties of touch, i.e. we are typically able to touch an object when it is near the body and after we have seen it.
To our knowledge, the effects of this proximity and habitual temporal order by which we perceive objects to the SOP have not been examined.
In addition, our study aimed to go beyond using questionnaires to measure the SOP.

Indeed, the validity of SOP questionnaires has been questioned from a theoretical standpoint, as post-task questionnaires rely on global, retrospective judgements while presence is seen as a property of immediate sensory experience (Sanchez-Vives & Slater, 2005; Slater, 2018).
text.formatted: Indeed, the validity of SOP questionnaires has been questioned from a theoretical standpoint, as post-task questionnaires rely on global, retrospective judgements while presence is seen as a property of immediate sensory experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Sanchez-Vives & Slater, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Slater, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A recent review found that in addition to this limitation, different presence questionnaires used different SOP definitions (Grassini & Laumann, 2020), which reduces the generalisability of findings across studies.
text.formatted: A recent review found that in addition to this limitation, different presence questionnaires used different SOP definitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Grassini & Laumann, 2020)</ref>, which reduces the generalisability of findings across studies.

text.text: To reduce some of the limitations associated with global, retrospective questionnaire measures of presence, our study used individual trial-by-trial ratings of whether the target stimulus was present within their environments.

These trial-by-trial VAS ratings allowed us also to assess individuals' confidence on their presence judgement and hence investigate differences between these conditions not only at the perceptual, but also the metacognitive level.
Specifically, metacognitive processes are defined as the monitoring, controlling and awareness of one's own cognitive processes without direct feedback from the environment (Flavell, 1979).
text.formatted: Specifically, metacognitive processes are defined as the monitoring, controlling and awareness of one's own cognitive processes without direct feedback from the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Flavell, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The extent to which the SOOP or the SOP are impacted by metacognitive processes is unknown and, as far as we are aware, untested in previous studies, despite the more general debates on the role of low-level perceptual processes, as opposed to topdown, cognitive influences (Fleming, 2024; Skarbez et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The extent to which the SOOP or the SOP are impacted by metacognitive processes is unknown and, as far as we are aware, untested in previous studies, despite the more general debates on the role of low-level perceptual processes, as opposed to topdown, cognitive influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fleming, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Skarbez et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It may be the case that because a greater sense of presence induces stronger perceptual representation of objects, that this will therefore lead to an improvement in metacognitive efficiency.
However, stronger perceptual signals do not necessarily lead to an increase in metacognitive efficiency, and vice versa (Fleming, 2024).
text.formatted: However, stronger perceptual signals do not necessarily lead to an increase in metacognitive efficiency, and vice versa <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fleming, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, our hypothesis that increased presence will correlate with an improved metacognitive performance is based on the nature of metacognition as a second-order computation about one's own performance, based on prior beliefs about the reliability and noise of one's own first order processing (Fleming & Daw, 2017).
text.formatted: Instead, our hypothesis that increased presence will correlate with an improved metacognitive performance is based on the nature of metacognition as a second-order computation about one's own performance, based on prior beliefs about the reliability and noise of one's own first order processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fleming & Daw, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because a virtual environment that generates a robust sense of presence is likely to be close to the ecological normality of the physical environment, we can therefore engage more ecologically normal metacognitive models instead of having to update existing models based on a new type of virtual environment.
This would mean that an increase in presence would also improve metacognitive efficiency.

Finally, our study will also collect reaction times to stimuli as a dependent variable to determine whether participants react faster in unisensory conditions involving touch versus vision, and corresponding multisensory manipulations.

Previous studies that have used reaction times as alternative, indirect measures of the SOP (Chandio et al., 2024; Hecht et al., 2006; Klimmt et al., 2005) have found negative correlations between reaction times and presence scores (e.g. Chandio et al., 2024), implying that people react faster to objects they experience as real.
text.formatted: Previous studies that have used reaction times as alternative, indirect measures of the SOP <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chandio et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hecht et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Klimmt et al., 2005)</ref> have found negative correlations between reaction times and presence scores (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chandio et al., 2024)</ref>, implying that people react faster to objects they experience as real.

text.text: Thus, our study uses three different measures to capture the SOP, namely trial-by-trial ratings and reaction times, and a global, validated SOP questionnaire.
We also controlled for key confounding parameter such as risk taking, ability to sustain attention over long periods of time, visual discrimination ability and touch discrimination ability.
Our study had three main hypotheses which were pre-registered on OSF prior to data collection (Registration ID: 10.17605/OSF.IO/SWUX2, accessible at https://osf.io/swux2/).
text.formatted: Our study had three main hypotheses which were pre-registered on OSF prior to data collection (Registration ID: 10.17605/OSF.IO/SWUX2, accessible at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/swux2/">https://osf.io/swux2/</ref>).

text.text: We hypothesise (1) that touch induces a greater sense of object presence than vision.

To test the possibility that touch's typical role as the last experienced sense impacts its relationship to the SOOP, we will vary the order by which participants experience objects in a multisensory capacity and compare reaction times to these conditions.
We therefore predict that (1a) touch-first multisensory trials will induce quicker reaction times than visionfirst multisensory trials.

We will also test the possibility that there is something specific about the nature of touch which induces a quicker understanding of object presence than vision by comparing reaction times between unisensory touch trials and unisensory vision trials.
We predict that (1b) touch unisensory trials will induce quicker reaction times than vision unisensory trials.

Secondly, we hypothesise that (2) although touch is the sense which produces the greatest increase in object presence, multisensory stimuli will always provide a greater sense of object presence than unisensory stimuli.
We will therefore compare confidence values between unisensory and multisensory conditions.

We predict that (2a) participants will exhibit greater metacognitive efficacy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials, and (2b) this will be accompanied with a higher overall accuracy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials.
Finally, we hypothesise that (3) a unisensory touch stimulus will provide a greater sense that an object is present than a unisensory visual stimulus.
We will therefore compare confidence values at identifying the presence of target stimuli between unisensory touch and unisensory vision conditions.

We predict that (3a) participants will exhibit greater metacognitive efficacy in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials, and (3b) be more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials.
The methodology, hypothesis and data analyses for this experiment was pre-registered on OSF prior to data collection (Registration ID: 10.17605/OSF.IO/SWUX2, accessible at https://osf.io/swux2/).
text.formatted: The methodology, hypothesis and data analyses for this experiment was pre-registered on OSF prior to data collection (Registration ID: 10.17605/OSF.IO/SWUX2, accessible at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/swux2/">https://osf.io/swux2/</ref>).

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
All data and analysis files, including videos of each VR block have been made publicly available on OSF and can be accessed at https://osf.io/5dzt7/files/osfstorage.
text.formatted: All data and analysis files, including videos of each VR block have been made publicly available on OSF and can be accessed at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/5dzt7/files/osfstorage">https://osf.io/5dzt7/files/osfstorage</ref>.

text.text: Data were analysed using R, version 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025), the packages tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), glmmTMB (Brooks et al., 2017), brms (Bürkner, 2017), bayestestR (Makowski et al., 2019) and psycho (Makowski, 2018).
text.formatted: Data were analysed using R, version 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025), the packages tidyverse <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Wickham et al., 2019)</ref>, lme4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>, glmmTMB <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brooks et al., 2017)</ref>, brms <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref>, bayestestR <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Makowski et al., 2019)</ref> and psycho <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Makowski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were automatically excluded from participating further in the study if they answered TRUE when asked if they had experienced a history of motion sickness in the demographics questionnaire.
No participants were excluded. 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male) were therefore recruited through the UCL SONA system.
The mean age of participants was 31.8 years (SD = 11.5).

An age distribution of 19 to 61 years significantly enhances the external validity and generalisability of our study, allowing us to investigate presence across adulthood rather than uniquely constrained to digital-native young adults.
Participants were aged 18 or above and provided informed consent before taking part in the study.
Each participant was remunerated a minimum of £13.50 with a chance to earn an extra £6 depending on task performance in the task (see below).
Our experiment employed a within-subjects design, in which we first manipulated the type of sensory modality participants experienced objects in VR within 2 levels, touch versus vision.
We also separately, manipulated the number of modalities presented to participants in 2 levels (Unisensory vs Multisensory).

Finally, in a third set of comparisons we tested the effects of temporal order in multisensory integration in two levels, we presented visuotactile stimuli to participants, but we presented either the touch or the vision stimuli half a second earlier (figure 1).
text.formatted: Finally, in a third set of comparisons we tested the effects of temporal order in multisensory integration in two levels, we presented visuotactile stimuli to participants, but we presented either the touch or the vision stimuli half a second earlier (figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: A graphical display of the conditions for our experimental design.
Our unisensory conditions were split into unisensory vision and unisensory touch, which were further split into either stimuli durations of 0.5s or 1s.
Our multisensory conditions were split into either Vision x Touch (vision appears 0.5s before touch) or Touch x Vision (touch appears 0.5s before vision).
The experiment is broken up into two blocks based on the dependent variable: a Reaction Time block and a Confidence block, counterbalanced between participants.

Reaction Time blocks measured perceptual accuracy and participant reaction time as the main dependent variables, whereas Confidence blocks collected perceptual accuracy and participant confidence as the main dependent variables.
We also collected global, post-task, presence scores as measured by the igroup Presence questionnaire (IPQ).

Although we are here measuring what we term as SOOP, there is not current validated questionnaire for this subset of SOP, and therefore the IPQ questionnaire will be used despite this minor theoretical difference.

We also collected four control measures to control for more basic, domain-general cognitive processes such as attention, and modality-specific discrimination abilities and RT, and also took into account participant age and VR familiarity into our analyses.

Specifically, Balloon Analogue Risk-Taking task (BART) score (Lejuez et al., 2002), Sustained Attention to Response task (SART) score (Stoet, 2010 (Stoet, , 2017)), a visual discrimination task (VDT) score and a touch discrimination task (HDT) score.
text.formatted: Specifically, Balloon Analogue Risk-Taking task (BART) score <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref>, Sustained Attention to Response task (SART) score <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Stoet, 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Stoet, , 2017))</ref>, a visual discrimination task (VDT) score and a touch discrimination task (HDT) score.

text.text: Self-reported age and VR and VR touch familiarity scores as the final two control variables.

The HDT and VDT were included to ensure that results were not confounded by a participant's individual difference in being able to discriminate a touch stimulus against other touch stimuli and being able to discriminate a visual stimulus from other visual stimuli.

The SART was included to minimise the impact of a participant's ability to sustain attention over a long period of time, since the main experiments involved long stretches of time completing the task in VR.

The BART score was included as a control since participant's general risk taking behaviour may influence the threshold at which they were sure enough that the target stimulus was present within their environments.

Age was included as people's reaction times tend to increase with age, and VR and VR haptics familiarity scores (how familiar participants were with VR and VR haptic technology on a scale of 0-5) were included as controls as participants with more experience in VR would feasibly do 'better' in both tasks than participants who were not as familiar with VR and had to learn the technology as they completed the task.
Sample size estimation was based on a power analysis performed on hypothesis 1 using G*Power3.1 (Faul et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Sample size estimation was based on a power analysis performed on hypothesis 1 using G*Power3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For our study, with Multisensory Order and Unisensory Modality (not their interaction) as our two main independent variables of interest regarding hypothesis 1, a moderate effect size of .4 (Barutchu & Spence, 2021), a power of .8, and alpha of .05, the recommended total sample size is 40 participants.

text.text: The moderate effect size utilised in this power calculation was based on a behavioural sensory-switching study undertaken by Barutchu & Spence (2021), since the core dependent variable (reaction time) and independent variables remain consistent with our study.

text.text: In total, we recruited and tested 44 participants (19-61 years, 27 female 17 male).
Our study utilised the Meta Quest 3 and its controllers to immerse participants within a VR environment.
Touch sensation was generated using https://www.ultraleap.com/ (previously UltraHaptics) HDK-REC192 touch device (Carter et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Touch sensation was generated using <ref type="url" target="https://www.ultraleap.com/">Ultraleap's</ref> (previously UltraHaptics) HDK-REC192 touch device <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carter et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This device utilises mid-air haptics to provide tactile feedback to users without the need for physical contact with an intermediary interface.
The haptic feedback is generated through the use of focused ultrasound.
The VR environment was created in-house using Unity 2023.2.15f1, with the Modular Caves asset bought from ProAssets in the Unity store.

Most VR studies which induce some kind of haptic feedback to the user do so either via controller vibration, vibrotactile stimulation via electrodes or mechanical stimulation via a glove-like device (Shi & Shen, 2024).
text.formatted: Most VR studies which induce some kind of haptic feedback to the user do so either via controller vibration, vibrotactile stimulation via electrodes or mechanical stimulation via a glove-like device <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Shi & Shen, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, each of these techniques includes the utilisation of some type of mediator to induce the feeling of touch (controller, electrode or glove).

The HDK_REC192 touch device allows for the simulation of touch without the need for a mediator to be attached to the skin, providing a more naturalistic experience of what it is like to reach out and touch an object in VR.

The device achieves this via a series of ultrasound generators, which work in synchronisation to project the sensation of touch onto the palm of the hand and can be programmed to induce the feeling of different shapes as well as movement.
The VR environment created was that of a cave system.
In the VR environment, participants are sat in the centre of a steel minecart travelling slowly along tracks within this cave system.
Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure 2).
text.formatted: Participants are also embodied within this stimulation -which is to say that when they looked down, they could see their own body sat in the same position as their body in the real world (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>).

text.text: To avoid any complications with discrepancies between the race and gender of the VR body and their real body, the VR body was covered in a brown jumpsuit.
Note.
An image of a participant in the real world (a) vs their perspective in the VR experience (b).
Participant body position is matched between VR and the real world.
The right arm of the participant is placed palm-up resting on a table in front of them, with the mid-air HDK_REC192 haptics device positioned above the centre of the palm.
Our Stimulus variable in each trial was either a target stimulus or a noise stimulus.

The target stimuli consisted of one type of visual stimulus (figure 3) and one type of touch stimulus (figure 4)(since these were the target stimuli), whereas the noise stimuli consisted of three different types of visual stimuli and three different types of touch stimuli.
text.formatted: The target stimuli consisted of one type of visual stimulus (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>) and one type of touch stimulus (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>)(since these were the target stimuli), whereas the noise stimuli consisted of three different types of visual stimuli and three different types of touch stimuli.

text.text: When multisensory conditions were presented to the participant, these were always congruentmeaning that the visual and touch stimuli presented were always of the same type.
In noise conditions, the visual and touch stimuli presented were also paired -meaning one type of visual noise stimulus was always paired with the same noise touch stimulus.
Both the types of stimuli and the conditions were presented to participants in a random order for 48 trials in total for each block (36 noise trials, 12 target trials).
Each stimulus (four total) was presented in each of the 12 conditions exactly once.
Note.
Visual stimuli presented to participants in the experimental tasks in order of distortion applied.
Stimulus 2 is the target stimulus, whilst stimuli 1, 3 and 4 are noise stimuli, created as distorted version of this target stimulus.
Note.
Touch stimuli presented to participants in the experimental tasks.
Stimulus 1 is the target stimulus participants were trained on.
Stimuli 2-4 were all noise stimuli.
In stimulus 1, a focal point is moving rapidly in a circular motion on the palm to give the illusion of a large circle.
In stimulus 2, a line moves at a moderate pace from bottom to top of the palm.
Both stimulus 3 and 4 are focal points which move at a moderate, circular pace.
Stimulus 3 has a larger circumference of movement than stimulus 4.
In this block, participants were told that the target stimuli they had been trained on was a species of Bat which was dangerous to humans.
Participants were tasked to remove the Bat from the cave by activating an inbuilt laser system by pressing the left index trigger on the left controller.
However, they were also told that this laser system could only be activated up to 20 times per day.
Participants were updated on how many laser activations they had remaining through a number shown to them in the VR headset.
Participants were also given a health bar which acted as an incentive for them to perform as well as possible during the task.
For every unit left on a participant's health bar at the end of the task, they would receive an extra 50 pence in compensation.
This gave participants a theoretical maximum of 19.5 pounds for their time (6 pounds for 12 health bar units left at the end of the task, plus the base pay of 13.5 pounds).
Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted.

Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block.
Participants wore ear defenders whilst completing the tasks to reduce any perception of noise created by the midair haptics device.
After completing the practice block, participants then moved on to the experimental block.
Once a stimulus from a random condition has been shown to the participant, the following scenario occurs:
The minecart stops moving, followed by a delay of 3 seconds.
If the participant thinks that the stimulus presented to them was the target stimulus, they choose to activate the laser and their screen flashes red.
If not, the participant does nothing.
If the participant correctly activates the laser, they lose no units of health, but their number of remaining laser activations reduces by 1.

If the participant incorrectly activates the laser (activates the laser when the stimulus presented was a noise stimulus), then they lose no health, but their remaining number of laser activations reduces by 1.
If a participant incorrectly does not activate the laser (does not activate the laser when a target stimulus was presented), their health bar reduces by 1 unit.
If the participant correctly does not activate the laser (does not activate the laser when a noise stimulus was presented), then neither their health bar nor their activations remaining is reduced.
Once 3 seconds has elapsed, the minecart begins moving again and the timer is reset, meaning that another stimulus will appear to the participant within a random interval of 5-15 seconds.
This cycle continues until each stimulus has appeared in each condition exactly twice, for a total of 48 trials.

If, at any point during the experimental block, a participant activated the laser so many times that they ended up with 0 laser shots remaining, they were told to disregard the fact they had 0 activations remaining and to carry on the task as normal.
A participant would have been told the same if their health bar also reached 0 at any point during the task.

In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure 5 for a summary of key differences).
text.formatted: In this block, participants were told that they would be giving explicit ratings as to whether the stimuli they experienced in VR were the same or different as compared to the learned target stimuli (see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">5</ref> for a summary of key differences).

text.text: Participants gave their answers on a confidence scale from 0-100, with 0 indicating a strong confidence that the stimulus just presented to them was the target stimulus, and 100 indicating that the stimulus just presented to them was not the target stimulus.

A participant's score on this scale allowed us to collect both their answer (whether the presented stimulus was the target stimulus or not) and their confidence in their answer (how far from 50 the participant rated the stimulus) at the same time.
Note.
The difference between our confidence block procedure (a) and reaction time block procedure (b).

In the confidence block, participants were asked to rate each stimulus following stimulus presentation, whereas in the reaction time block participants were asked to react by pressing a button if they thought they experienced the target stimulus.
Before starting the task, participants were allowed to familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 30 seconds uninterrupted.

Participants were then allowed to re-familiarise themselves with the target stimuli for 5 seconds before undertaking the practice block, and then for another 5 seconds before undertaking the experimental block.
Participants wore ear defenders whilst completing the tasks to reduce any perception of noise created by the midair haptics device.
After completing the practice block, participants then moved on to the experimental block.
Once a stimulus from a random condition has been shown to the participant, the following scenario occurs:
The minecart stops moving, followed by a delay of 3 seconds.
Once 3 seconds has elapsed, a slider appears in front of the participant in VR, with Same on one end of the slider and Different on the other end.
The participant then rates their confidence regarding whether they think that the stimulus just shown to them was the same or different from the target stimulus.
This is done using the thumb stick on the left controller.
Once a participant is happy with their rating, they press the X button on the left controller to confirm their answer.

Once the X button has been pressed their data is recorded, and the slider is reset to a random value between 0-100 and the timer starts again -meaning the participant will now wait for another 5-15 seconds before being presented with the next stimulus.
These random values were not recorded or controlled for in the final analyses, since the random nature of the reset slider should provide adequate control for anchoring effects here.

Once participants have finished both experimental VR blocks, they are then presented with a questionnaire to collect our dependent variable Presence Score and additional control variables of VR and VR Touch familiarity scores.
This questionnaire includes items from the IPQ (Schubert et al., 2001) as well as some custom items.
text.formatted: This questionnaire includes items from the IPQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Schubert et al., 2001)</ref> as well as some custom items.

text.text: For more information, please refer to the supplementary materials.

To first determine whether reaction times in the reaction time task negatively correlated with presence scores measured by the presence questionnaire, we will conduct an exploratory linear mixed-effects model with mean reaction time per conditions as our dependent variable, using average presence score per participant as our other dependent variable of interest.
We will include random effects here for ID and Condition.
We will also do the same to determine whether confidence in the confidence task positively correlates with presence scores measured by the presence questionnaire.

We will conduct another linear mixed-effects model, using metacognitive efficacy as our dependent variable and presence scores as our independent variable of interest with random effects for ID and Condition.

If either of these correlations is non-significant, we will conduct a Bayes equivalence test to determine whether these results are truly negative (Stanton, 2021), thus providing us with useful information regarding the utilisation of either reaction time or confidence as behavioural measures of presence.
text.formatted: If either of these correlations is non-significant, we will conduct a Bayes equivalence test to determine whether these results are truly negative <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Stanton, 2021)</ref>, thus providing us with useful information regarding the utilisation of either reaction time or confidence as behavioural measures of presence.

text.text: We will determine whether touch-first multisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision-first multisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. This model included Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects, with the log of Mean Reaction Time as our dependent variable of interest.
The model also included random intercepts for ID.
We also pre-registered including differences in signal conduction velocity between the visual and touch sensory systems as a control in our analyses.
We were unable to find any reliable literature on this; therefore we are excluding this control variable from all our analyses.

We will also not be controlling for scores in the Wisconsin Card Sorting task (WCST), since we decided that behavioural measures in this task would not capture any significant mental processes which would confound the results in our experiment.

Analysis 1b -We will determine whether touch unisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. This model included Modality (our unisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch or Visual), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables with the log of Mean Reaction Time as our dependent variable of interest.
The model also included random intercepts for ID and Stimulus Duration.
We will determine whether participants exhibited greater metacognitive efficacy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model.
Our pre-registered analyses included calculating m-ratio from confidence and accuracy values generated in the Confidence block.
However, we were unable to generate these figures using the most optimal method since we did not have enough signal trials per condition per participant.

Therefore, we created a replacement measure for metacognition in which we correlated accuracy on the confidence task with reported confidence, giving us a score for each participant per object per condition.
We used our replacement measure for metacognition as our dependent variable, with Sense (unisensory or multisensory) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.

Analysis 2b -We will determine whether participants exhibited a higher overall accuracy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used Accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Sense (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Multisensory or Unisensory), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables.
We also included ID and Duration as random effects variables.

We will determine whether unisensory touch scenarios induced a significantly greater metacognitive efficacy than unisensory visual trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used metacognition as our dependent variable, with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.

Analysis 3b -We will determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials by using a linear mixed-effects model using the lme4 package in R. We used accuracy as our dependent variable (d' values calculated using the psycho package in R, a deviation from our pre-registered analyses), with Modality (our independent variable of interest with 2 levels: Touch or Vision), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.

For our core experimental analyses (Hypotheses 1, 2, and 3), statistical thresholds will be kept at p=0.05 without broad multi-test corrections, as each model evaluates independent, a priori pre-registered hypotheses addressing distinct psychological mechanisms.

While Hypotheses 2b and 3b share the same underlying accuracy metrics (d'), they evaluate orthogonal statistical effects (the macro-effect of multisensory integration vs the effect of sensory modality within unisensory contexts, respectively).
Applying broad adjustments across conceptually independent primary models would over-penalize the architecture and artificially inflate Type II error rates.

However, for post-hoc exploratory comparisons involving repeated lookups on the same data array (e.g., the questionnaire items in Exploratory Analysis 4), an explicit Bonferroni correction is applied to control family-wise error rates.

text.text: We first conducted an exploratory linear mixed-effects model to determine whether mean reaction time -our main dependent variable of interest for hypothesis 1 -could be predicted by self-reported presence levels.

To achieve this, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using the log of mean reaction time as our dependent variable, with average presence score and age as our fixed effects variables and ID and Condition as our random effects variables.
We found that, in all sensory conditions, an increase in presence score significantly negatively correlated with reaction time (𝜷 = -.09, SE = .033, t = -2.74, p = .006) (see figure 6).
text.formatted: We found that, in all sensory conditions, an increase in presence score significantly negatively correlated with reaction time (𝜷 = -.09, SE = .033, t = -2.74, p = .006) (see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">6</ref>).

text.text: Note.
The relationships between each participant's presence score and their mean reaction time in each condition during the Reaction Time task.
The x axis represents Presence score, whereas the Y axis represents raw Mean Reaction Time.

Presence score displays a significant negative correlation with mean reaction time, suggesting that participants who felt greater overall presence within the VR environment also displayed faster reaction times regardless of condition.
We also wanted to determine whether participant metacognition score (a correlation between accuracy and confidence scores in the confidence block) correlated with levels of presence.

To do this, we conducted another linear mixed effect model with metacognition as our dependent variable, Average Presence Score as our fixed effects variable and ID and Condition as our random effects variables.
We found no correlation between metacognition scores and presence scores in any condition (𝜷 = .0184, SE = .0558, t(31) = .33, p = .743).
To ensure that the correlation was truly null, we conducted a Bayes equivalence test on our linear mixed-effects model.
Our null hypothesis posited that there was no correlation between metacognition scores and presence scores within the predefined bounds of [-.1,.1].

The test produced a Bayes factor of BF01 = 268, indicating overwhelming evidence in favour of the null hypothesis, suggesting that the relationship between metacognitive scores and presence in our study is null.
We aimed to determine whether touch-first multisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision-first multisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model.

We found no significant difference in mean reaction times between conditions in which Touch was presented for .5 seconds before vision and conditions in which vision was presented for .5 seconds before Touch (𝜷 = -.02, SE = .052, t(37.4) = -.38, p = .71) (table 1).
text.formatted: We found no significant difference in mean reaction times between conditions in which Touch was presented for .5 seconds before vision and conditions in which vision was presented for .5 seconds before Touch (𝜷 = -.02, SE = .052, t(37.4) = -.38, p = .71) (table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We aimed to determine whether touch unisensory trials induced quicker reaction times than vision unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model.

We found that, contrary to our hypothesis, participants exhibited significantly faster reaction times in unisensory visual trials compared to unisensory touch trials (𝜷 = -.18, SE = .04, t(102.6) = -4.6, p < .001).
text.formatted: We found that, contrary to our hypothesis, participants exhibited significantly faster reaction times in unisensory visual trials compared to unisensory touch trials (𝜷 = -.18, SE = .04, t(102.6) = -4.6, p < .001).

The model includes random intercepts for ID and Duration, and BART score, SART score, Touch score, Vision score and Age as control variables.
Unisensory visual scenarios were found to predict a significantly lower reaction time than unisensory touch scenarios.
We also found a significant positive relationship between BART scores and reaction time.
We aimed to determine whether participants exhibited greater metacognitive efficacy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model.

This analysis found that participants exhibited significantly less metacognitive efficacy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions with multisensory serving as the reference baseline (𝜷 = -.149, SE = .0549, t(33.1) = -2.71, p = .011).
We aimed to determine whether participants exhibited a higher overall accuracy in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials using a linear mixed-effects model.
We found that participants exhibited a significantly reduced perceptual sensitivity in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory modalities (𝜷 = -.553, SE = .055, z = -10.12, p < .001).
