The non-normality of error terms for d' were also verified using simulated residuals, with inspection of the error distribution Therefore, we decided to perform an additional exploratory analysis by first normalising and adjusting the d' values using the following formulae: 𝑑′𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 = (𝑑′ -𝑚𝑖𝑛(𝑑′)) / (𝑚𝑎𝑥(𝑑′) -𝑚𝑖𝑛(𝑑′)) 𝑑′𝐴𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑑 = 𝑑′𝑁𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑙 × (1 -2 * 1 × 10 -6 ) + 1 × 10 -6

Once we had obtained adjusted d' scores for each condition for each subject, we then utilised the glmmTMB package within R to allow us to devise a new linear mixed-effects model which accounts for the beta distribution of the adjusted d' scores -our new dependent variable of interest.

Using this model, whist keeping the fixed and random effects constant from the previously described model, we again found a significant decrease in accuracy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions (𝜷 = -.1, SE = .011, z = -9.14, p < .001).

text.text: To verify that the model's error structures were valid, we evaluated the simulated residuals using the DHARMa package.

The resulting residual plots and Q-Q plots confirmed that once the non-normal skew of the data was absorbed by the Beta distribution, the model's errors conformed to the expected distribution and free of systematic bias.

To ensure that the impact of our asymmetrical target-to-noise ratio (25% target trials) did not impact participant decision strategies and therefore d', we conducted a further analysis on the signal detection criterion (c) generated via the psycho package in R. The sample exhibited a consistently conservative baseline response criterion (M = 0.15, SD = 0.57, Median = 0.24).
A linear model tracking criterion values across experimental conditions revealed no significant main effect of condition on response bias, F(5, 1050) = 1.93, p = .087, R² adj = .004.
This indicates that our conservative response bias, caused by asymmetrical trial numbers, did not systematically interact with our experimental contrasts using d' as our dependent variable.

To determine whether unisensory touch scenarios induced a significantly greater metacognitive efficacy than unisensory visual trials, we used our previously calculated correlations between participant Response Accuracy (whether or not they correctly identified or correctly rejected the presence of the target stimulus) with Confidence for each condition (as described in exploratory hypothesis 2a).
Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value.
This resulted in 55 error values, leaving us with 121 observations.

Once we had obtained these correlations, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using our newly created correlations as our dependent variable, with Sense (unisensory touch or unisensory vision) as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.

This exploratory analysis found no significant difference in metacognitive efficacy between unisensory visual and touch conditions with unisensory touch serving as the reference baseline (𝜷 = .117, SE = .0614, t(98.3) = 1.9, p = .06), with the non-significant numerical trend leaning toward higher monitoring efficiency in vision.
However, It should be noted that the large number of exclusions may make these results weaker than they appear.
We also aimed to determine whether participants were more accurate in touch unisensory trials compared to visual unisensory trials.
Similarly to our methodology in our exploratory hypothesis 2b analysis, we normalised the calculated d' variables before analysis, since they exhibited a significant positive skew.

After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table 4).
text.formatted: After adjustment, we then performed the linear mixedeffects model using these values and found that participants were significantly less accurate in unisensory vision conditions compared to unisensory touch conditions (𝜷 = -.032, SE = .011, t(641) = -3, p = .0028) (table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

We wanted to determine whether there was any difference in participant reaction times to unisensory or multisensory stimuli.

To do this, we utilised another linear mixed-effects model using the log of reaction time as our dependent variable, with Integration (unisensory or multisensory), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control) and Age as our fixed effects variables.
We also included ID and Duration as random effects variables.
We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001).
text.formatted: We found that participants were significantly slower at identifying the presence of the target in unisensory trials compared to multisensory trials (𝜷 = .127, SE = .0334, t(179) = 3.81, p < .001).

text.text: We also found a significant positive correlation between BART score and reaction time (𝜷 = .0834, SE = .0386, t(34.8) = 2.16, p = .0379).
We wanted to determine whether there was a difference in metacognitive efficacy between our two multisensory trials -TouchxVision and VisionxTouch.

To do this, we utilised our previously calculated correlations between participant Response Accuracy (whether or not they correctly identified or correctly rejected the presence of the target stimulus) with Confidence for each condition (as described in exploratory hypothesis 2a).
Since we had 12 observations per participant, some participants were able to get over 90% of trials correct, meaning a correlation between their accuracy and confidence resulted in an error value.
This resulted in 42 error values, leaving us with 46 observations.

Once we had obtained these correlations, we conducted a linear mixed-effects model using our newly created correlations as our dependent variable, with Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), as our independent variable of interest and ID as a random effects variable.
This exploratory analysis found no significant difference in metacognitive efficacy between our multisensory conditions (𝜷 = -.014, SE = .12, t(44) = -.12, p = .91).
However, It should be noted that the large number of exclusions may make these results weaker than they appear.
We wanted to determine whether there was a difference in accuracy between our two multisensory trials -TouchxVision and VisionxTouch.
To do this, we utilised the previously calculated d' variables which were normalised prior to analysis.

After adjustment, we then performed a linear mixed-effects model using these values as our dependent variable and Integration (our multisensory independent variables of interest with 2 levels -Touch then Visual and Visual then Touch), BART score (continuous control), SART score (continuous control), Visual discrimination score (continuous control), Touch discrimination score (continuous control), Age, VR Familiarity and VR Touch Familiarity as our fixed effects variables and ID as a random effects variable.

We found that participants were significantly less accurate in multisensory scenarios in which vision appeared before touch than in scenarios where touch appeared before vision (𝜷 = -.037, SE = .011, t(297.93) = -3.32, p = .001**).
We included a final 3 items at the end of the presence questionnaire undertaken by participants which were not in the original questionnaire developed by Schubert et al. (2001).
text.formatted: We included a final 3 items at the end of the presence questionnaire undertaken by participants which were not in the original questionnaire developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schubert et al. (2001)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these 3 items asked participants how real they felt each type of scenario was (Unisensory Touch, Unisensory Vision and Multisensory).
To determine which sensory scenario participants felt was the most real, we conducted a series of paired t-tests comparing scores on these items.
This series was corrected for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction, resulting in a significance threshold of p = 0.0167.
Our first t-test compared scores on the Touch question against the Vision question.
This ttest found that participants felt that the touch scenarios were significantly more real than the vision scenarios (t(43)=5.52, p < .001).
text.formatted: This ttest found that participants felt that the touch scenarios were significantly more real than the vision scenarios (t(43)=5.52, p < .001).

text.text: Our second t-test compared scores on the Vision question against the Multisensory question.
This t-test found that participants felt that the visual scenarios were significantly less real than the multisensory conditions (t(43)=-4.98, p < .001).
text.formatted: This t-test found that participants felt that the visual scenarios were significantly less real than the multisensory conditions (t(43)=-4.98, p < .001).

text.text: Our third t-test compared scores on the Touch question against the Multisensory question.
This t-test found that participants felt that the touch scenarios were significantly more real than the multisensory conditions (t(43)=2.94, p = .005).

This indicates that participants felt that touch scenarios were the most real, followed by multisensory conditions and vision scenarios as the least real.
The broad aim of this study was to investigate the impact of touch on the SOOP in VR.

We had three main hypotheses: (1) touch induces a greater SOOP than vision, (2) multisensory stimuli will always provide a greater SOOP than unisensory stimuli and (3) a unisensory touch stimulus will provide a greater SOOP than a unisensory visual stimulus.

Hypotheses 1 and 3 remain unsupported, since touch did not induce a significantly greater SOOP than vision in either multisensory or unisensory contexts, but hypothesis 2 is supported since multisensory stimuli did provide a greater SOOP than unisensory stimuli.
However, we also found significant findings with regards to differences between behavioural results between touch and vision stimuli and questionnaire results.

Our study is the first to our knowledge to operationalise and measure different facets of the multidimensional concept of the SOOP, ranging from indirect, trial-by-trial measures of reaction times and accuracy to higher-order aspects of presence judgements such as their trial-by-trial metacognitive efficiency, and to modality-specific and modality-general global (i.e. across many trials), retrospective selfreport measures.
By examining our central hypotheses on all our measures, we were able to account for the role of touch on the SOOP as a multidimensional construct.
To investigate our hypotheses, we wanted to utilise comparisons between behavioural measures of presence: reaction time and metacognitive efficacy.
Therefore, we investigated whether presence scores, as measured by the IPQ questionnaire, correlated with reaction time and metacognitive efficacy.

The current study found that presence scores increased significantly as reaction time decreased -meaning that we can use reaction times from our reaction time block as behavioural predictors of presence.
However, we found no relationship between presence scores and metacognition as calculated in the analysis described in section 3.2.
We further investigated this relationship by utilising a Bayesian equivalence test, which confirmed the results as truly null.
It is important to re-iterate here that some of our analyses deviated significantly from our preregistered protocols -specifically any analysis using either d' or m-ratio as a dependent variable.
Originally, we planned to use a Bayesian estimation method to generate both d' and m-ratio values via the metadpy Python toolbox (Embodied Cognition Group, 2023).
However, the parameter estimates generated by this modelling framework over our low trialto-condition ratio introduced severe mathematical artifacts.
To calculate m-ratio in this way, responses must be binned into a minimum number of categories.

Since we had a low number of observations per participant per condition, many of these bins ended up empty, causing artefacts when meta-d' was calculated and, therefore, resulting in the generation of multiple impossible final m-ratio numbers (negative values and values well above 1 (e.g. one participant in particular scored an m-ratio of 11.23 -1123% metacognitive efficiency).
Had we used this data for our analyses, we would've had to exclude 13 out of our 44 participants.
Therefore, to preserve statistical validity, we implemented alternative computational approaches.

For our exploratory analysis of perceptual sensitivity, d' variables were generated using the psycho package in R, which calculates sensitivity directly from unbinned raw trial counts (Hits, Misses, False Alarms, and Correct Rejections).
This was paired with a beta-distribution GLMM framework (glmmTMB) to account for the heavy positive skew and bounded nature of our accuracy data.

Furthermore, because individual m-ratio modelling collapsed entirely under zero-cell counts, it was replaced in our exploratory analyses with a non-parametric index of metacognitive monitoring generated via trial-by-trial, within-subject correlations between confidence and objective accuracy.

While we acknowledge this replacement measure is inherently noisier and susceptible to data loss when performance is invariant, it provides a robust window into metacognitive monitoring without forcing rigid parametric assumptions onto sparse data.

Consequently, this discussion focuses primarily on the results generated from these distribution-corrected variables, while the original, pre-registered modelling outputs can be found in the supplementary materials.
Regarding our replacement measure of metacognitive efficiency, we cannot draw any further conclusions regarding the relationship between our independent variables and the sense of presence in VR.
This is because we found no significant correlation between metacognitive efficiency and global presence scores.
This may be for a number of reasons.
Firstly, there was a limitation within our experiment regarding the gamification of blocks.
Although the reaction time block was gamified, in that participants won more money for performing better, the metacognition block was not.

This may have introduced a confound that meant participants cared less and therefore performed worse in the confidence block, causing our measure of metacognition to no longer correlate with presence.

However, there is ample evidence in psychology to suggest that although gamification is one method to ensure participants maintain attention and concentration on the set task, it is not the only method, and other general rewards as well as the satisfaction of successfully completing a task to the best of one's ability are also sufficient (Hanks & Summerfield, 2017; Harvey et al., 2024; James et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, there is ample evidence in psychology to suggest that although gamification is one method to ensure participants maintain attention and concentration on the set task, it is not the only method, and other general rewards as well as the satisfaction of successfully completing a task to the best of one's ability are also sufficient <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hanks & Summerfield, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Harvey et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">James et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Secondly, previous research regarding the relationship between metacognitive processes and the sense of reality has similar results.

One recent study (Dijkstra et al., 2024) attempted to define the relationship between metacognition and the sense of reality through the lens of perceptual reality monitoring -the ability to distinguish between internally generated content and external perceptual phenomena (Lau, 2019).
text.formatted: One recent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dijkstra et al., 2024)</ref> attempted to define the relationship between metacognition and the sense of reality through the lens of perceptual reality monitoring -the ability to distinguish between internally generated content and external perceptual phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lau, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, the authors attempted to determine whether participants demonstrated insight into whether their judgments regarding the origins of perceptual stimulation (either internally or externally generated) were correct.
This study found that, although participants had some limited global, task-level insight into their performance, this was uncorrelated with the triallevel insight measured during the task.
Therefore, trial-by-trial confidence ratings do not distinguish between imagination and reality during perceptual tasks.

It is therefore clear that, in this case, the accuracy of metacognitive judgements does not fully depend on the same signal parameters or cognitive processes as those that determine perceptual performance (Fleming, 2024).
text.formatted: It is therefore clear that, in this case, the accuracy of metacognitive judgements does not fully depend on the same signal parameters or cognitive processes as those that determine perceptual performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fleming, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although our two studies are underlined with different theoretical frameworks (the current study was not designed and draws no conclusion regarding perceptual reality monitoring), our finding that trial-level measures of metacognitive efficiency were not correlated with a participant's sense of presence seems parallel to findings both in the field of perceptual reality monitoring and more broad theoretical conceptions of metacognition as being dissociable from task performance.
Measures of metacognition are therefore not likely to perform as good measures of presence.
We found no difference in either reaction times or metacognitive efficacy when comparing our multisensory conditions VisionxTouch and TouchxVision.
This was an unexpected finding.

We hypothesised that participants would react faster in touch-first multisensory conditions compared to vision-first multisensory conditions, and that this would be accompanied by an increase in metacognitive efficacy.

This hypothesis was based on previous studies which suggested that touch alone contributed more to the sense of presence than vision alone (Gibbs et al., 2022), and also empirical and theoretical investigations of touch and its role in perception and action (Massin, 2009; Serino, 2019 Serino, , 2022)).
text.formatted: This hypothesis was based on previous studies which suggested that touch alone contributed more to the sense of presence than vision alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gibbs et al., 2022)</ref>, and also empirical and theoretical investigations of touch and its role in perception and action <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Massin, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Serino, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Serino, , 2022))</ref>.

text.text: Considering this research, we expected a multisensory, visuo-haptic condition in which we presented touch slightly before vision to induce a greater sense of presence faster than a visuo-haptic condition in which we presented vision before touch.
However, our results suggest that this is not the case, and that there is no difference between these two conditions.

This may simply be because the presentation of vision and touch together, regardless as to which was presented first, is more than enough of a sensory signal to determine that an object is present within one's environment.

In support of hypothesis 2, we found that participants demonstrated significantly faster reaction times, greater accuracy and increased metacognitive ability in multisensory trials compared to unisensory trials, meaning participants felt that multisensory objects were present within their environments faster than unisensory objects.

This result is a replication of previous findings in the field of human-computer interaction, which consistently find that multisensory experiences induce greater presence for individuals in VR than unisensory experiences.

Multiple previous studies and meta analyses have found significant differences in how present participants feel in VR environments when the environment is purely visual vs multisensory, with participants always feeling more present in multisensory environments (Gallace et al., 2012; Melo et al., 2022; Schwind et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Multiple previous studies and meta analyses have found significant differences in how present participants feel in VR environments when the environment is purely visual vs multisensory, with participants always feeling more present in multisensory environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gallace et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Melo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Schwind et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although our result here is just a replication of previous findings, this provides some validity to our paradigm.
This is particularly important, since our experimental paradigm involves the usage of a novel haptic medium -mid-air haptics.
Typically, haptic stimulation is deployed to participants in VR via some kind of intermediary mechanism.
Such mechanisms typically include haptic gloves (Perret & Vander Poorten, 2018), controller vibrations (Våpenstad et al., 2013) or other types of vibrotactile stimulators (Hwang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such mechanisms typically include haptic gloves <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Perret & Vander Poorten, 2018)</ref>, controller vibrations <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Våpenstad et al., 2013)</ref> or other types of vibrotactile stimulators <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hwang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, experiencing vibrotactile feedback via an intermediary controller is not necessarily naturalistic since the feeling of the intermediary controller on the skin impacts the overall haptic experience.

In theory, novel mid-air haptics presents a more naturalistic way for participants in VR to experience tactile feedback from objects since there is no intermediary contact with the participant's skin.

Our finding that participants were faster in multisensory scenarios compared to unisensory scenarios suggests that, despite the novelty of mid-air haptics, multisensory mechanisms were still recruited when participants were presented with a visual stimulus accompanied by a haptic stimulus produced via novel mid-air haptics.
Our results also show that participants were faster at responding to the presence of target objects in unisensory vision trials compared to unisensory touch trials.
This finding is in opposition to hypothesis 1.

This is in spite of the fact that mean haptic reaction times tend to be slightly faster than mean visual reaction times (155ms vs 180-200ms) (Fieandt, 1956; Wang et al., 2022; Welford & Brebner, 1980).
text.formatted: This is in spite of the fact that mean haptic reaction times tend to be slightly faster than mean visual reaction times (155ms vs 180-200ms) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fieandt, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Wang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Welford & Brebner, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: It may be that we feel as if touch confirms an object's presence in our environments due to the fact that the addition of touch to vision merely recruits multisensory mechanisms, which then go on to improve our sense that the object is present (Cooper et al., 2018; Gallace et al., 2012; Marucci et al., 2021), and that there is no special role of touch.
text.formatted: It may be that we feel as if touch confirms an object's presence in our environments due to the fact that the addition of touch to vision merely recruits multisensory mechanisms, which then go on to improve our sense that the object is present <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cooper et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Gallace et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Marucci et al., 2021)</ref>, and that there is no special role of touch.

text.text: However, there is a significant confound within our methodology that caveats this conclusion.

Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception (Fan et al., 2020; Mayeli, 2019; Stokes & Biggs, 2014) by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision.
text.formatted: Although our experiment attempted to attenuate the role of visual dominance in perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mayeli, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Stokes & Biggs, 2014)</ref> by presenting target touch and target visual stimuli to participants in a random order, meaning they must attend equally to both tactile and visual information, it is likely that the addition of visual-only task-relevant information (the counter for the number of shots the participant had remaining, and the red health bar which indicated how many target stimuli the participant had missed) may have shifted attention, and therefore perceptual dominance in the task, towards vision.

text.text: This would bias reaction times in favour of the visual stimuli.
This is a clear limitation which reduces confidence in our rejection of hypothesis 1 and warrants a replication where this limitation is removed.
However, this caveated conclusion would be in opposition to the results of items on our modified presence questionnaire.

When asked specifically which condition felt most real to them during the experiment (touch, vision or multisensory), participants rated touch as feeling significantly more real than both multisensory and vision conditions and rated multisensory conditions as more real than visual conditions.

We first hypothesise that participants rated touch as feeling significantly more real than multisensory scenarios due to the fact that all of the multisensory conditions were temporally incongruent (vision presented either 500ms before touch, or touch 500ms before vision).
We also hypothesise that this difference between touch and vision means that there is a difference between the online sense of presence and a post-hoc judgment of the same sense.

It is important, especially when investigating concepts such as the SOP and SOOP, to distinguish between the moment of the original, real experience (the perception of a stimulus in VR) and the judgments based around it (presence questionnaires administered outside of VR) (Blankenburg, 1971; Jaspers, 1913).
text.formatted: It is important, especially when investigating concepts such as the SOP and SOOP, to distinguish between the moment of the original, real experience (the perception of a stimulus in VR) and the judgments based around it (presence questionnaires administered outside of VR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blankenburg, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jaspers, 1913)</ref>.

text.text: Put more simply, although presence questionnaires may give us accurate measures of post-hoc judgments of presence, they do not give us insight into a participants' immediate perceptual awareness of presence.

Since the definition of presence is rooted in its impact on immediate phenomenology (Burdea & Coiffet, 2024), this raises further questions about how to incorporate other measures besides questionnaires into experiments attempting to measure presence (Usoh et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Since the definition of presence is rooted in its impact on immediate phenomenology <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Burdea & Coiffet, 2024)</ref>, this raises further questions about how to incorporate other measures besides questionnaires into experiments attempting to measure presence <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Usoh et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, it may be that differences between behavioural and questionnaire measures of presence are due to the nature of the virtual stimuli and the environment.
Recent thinking in the field of cognitive neuroscience has placed emphasis on the way in which we present stimuli to participants.

In a vast majority of cases, the stimuli used in these experiments are proxies of realism (Snow & Culham, 2021) -by which we mean 2D or 3D images meant to represent real-world stimuli (for an example of this, see Magritte's famous work "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" (Magritte & Torczyner, 1994)).
text.formatted: In a vast majority of cases, the stimuli used in these experiments are proxies of realism <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Snow & Culham, 2021)</ref> -by which we mean 2D or 3D images meant to represent real-world stimuli (for an example of this, see Magritte's famous work "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Magritte & Torczyner, 1994)</ref>).

text.text: In our case, and the case of other experiments using both VR headsets alongside haptic stimulation, the stimuli presented to participants in VR are not mere proxies for reality, but as close to real objects as one could feasibly get whilst controlling for various confounding variables within an experimental context (Singleton & Fotopoulou, 2026).
text.formatted: In our case, and the case of other experiments using both VR headsets alongside haptic stimulation, the stimuli presented to participants in VR are not mere proxies for reality, but as close to real objects as one could feasibly get whilst controlling for various confounding variables within an experimental context <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Singleton & Fotopoulou, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It may be the case that 3D virtual renderings of objects in an embodied space produce faster reaction time measures in visual conditions because the brain utilizes isolated visual input as a highly efficient, feedforward spatial radar to initiate rapid motor choices (Gomez et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It may be the case that 3D virtual renderings of objects in an embodied space produce faster reaction time measures in visual conditions because the brain utilizes isolated visual input as a highly efficient, feedforward spatial radar to initiate rapid motor choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gomez et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, haptic feedback provides greater perceptual accuracy and retrospective judgements of 'realness' because interacting with an actionable, tangible asset recruits distinct mechanisms that satisfy the brain's evolutionary requirements for physical interaction and object solidity (Snow & Culham, 2021).
text.formatted: Conversely, haptic feedback provides greater perceptual accuracy and retrospective judgements of 'realness' because interacting with an actionable, tangible asset recruits distinct mechanisms that satisfy the brain's evolutionary requirements for physical interaction and object solidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Snow & Culham, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms (Gomez et al., 2018; Snow & Culham, 2021).
text.formatted: This may explain why participants had a greater accuracy at identifying virtual objects via haptics alone and also reported these objects as feeling more real, though they were slower at reacting to them since the 'realness' of the object compared to the 3D visual-only render recruited a wider assortment of brain mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gomez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Snow & Culham, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This raises significant questions about how best to experimentally measure concepts such as presence as well as implement multimodal virtual environments, since presence relies on the subject feeling as if they are in a real environment and interacting with real objects.

Although we found no difference in metacognitive ability between unisensory touch and unisensory visual trials in our confidence block, exploratory analysis 3b did find that participants were significantly more accurate in unisensory touch trials compared to unisensory visual trials.
This lends some very limited support to hypothesis 3, though the lack of a significant difference regarding metacognitive ability means that we should also reject this hypothesis.
However, we also found that participants were more accurate in multisensory conditions where touch was presented before vision than conditions in which vision was presented before touch.

Importantly, these findings cannot be explained by any subjective or objective difference in difficulty in discriminating between noise and target visual and touch trials, since these factors were controlled for in two control tasks (VDT and HDT) administered prior to the experiment.

These findings to be consistent with previous literature, in that touch has been found to induce greater confidence about the identity of objects than vision in cases where the object is perceptually ambiguous (Fairhurst et al., 2018; Wijntjes et al., 2009).
text.formatted: These findings to be consistent with previous literature, in that touch has been found to induce greater confidence about the identity of objects than vision in cases where the object is perceptually ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fairhurst et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Wijntjes et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Since both our visual and haptic stimuli were designed to be perceptually ambiguous, it seems plausible that participants would therefore be more accurate at identifying ambiguous stimuli via touch than via vision.

These findings also suggest that although we utilised novel technology to deliver the feeling of touch to participants in VR, that this novelty did not negatively impact participants ability to discern between target and non-target stimuli through touch.
This provides some level of validation for the materials used in the experiment.

Our finding that participants exhibited significantly lower metacognitive efficacy and less accuracy in unisensory conditions compared to multisensory conditions is consistent with previous literature from the field, lending some validity to our paradigm.

Multiple previous studies testing participant response in a variety of experimental paradigms, including reaction times, discriminatory ability and perceptual accuracy (Cooper et al., 2018; Marucci et al., 2021; Uemae et al., 2015) have found that, broadly, participants perform better in tasks in which they are given multisensory cues compared to unisensory cues.
text.formatted: Multiple previous studies testing participant response in a variety of experimental paradigms, including reaction times, discriminatory ability and perceptual accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cooper et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Marucci et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Uemae et al., 2015)</ref> have found that, broadly, participants perform better in tasks in which they are given multisensory cues compared to unisensory cues.

text.text: However, fewer studies have investigated the role of metacognition in incoming multisensory vs unisensory perceptual information (Kimmet et al., 2023; Meijer & Noppeney, 2023).
text.formatted: However, fewer studies have investigated the role of metacognition in incoming multisensory vs unisensory perceptual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kimmet et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Meijer & Noppeney, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our finding that participants experienced greater metacognitive efficacy regarding perceptual discrimination in visuo-touch conditions compared to vision-only or touch-only conditions may be a significant contribution to the field of multisensory integration.

Additionally, although we did find that multisensory conditions increased presence, reaction time and accuracy over unisensory conditions, these results may understate the true impact of congruent multisensory stimuli on presence since our multisensory stimuli were always temporally incongruent.
Future studies could address these limitations in a number of ways.
First, future studies intending to investigate similar questions regarding the relative importance of touch vs vision on the sense of presence should be careful to match visual and touch dominance.
Importantly, avoiding any task-relevant information which is only presented in one sensory domain.
Secondly, it may be of interest to the field as a whole for future studies to attempt to decipher the role of task engagement in the creation of the sense of presence.

If undertaking different types of task within the same virtual environment causes shifts in how present a participant feels within the VR simulation, this may have crucial implications when it comes to translating psychological research undertaken in VR into real-world applications.

This study investigated the relative contributions of touch and vision to the Sense of Object Presence (SOOP) in VR, utilizing novel mid-air haptic technology (ultrasound) to simulate tactile feedback without physical intermediaries.

Across a sample of 44 participants, we employed a rigorous dual-paradigm approach, contrasting implicit behavioural measures (reaction times verified against attention and risk-taking controls) with explicit metacognitive judgments.
Our results confirmed that multisensory integration significantly enhances metacognitive efficacy, accuracy, and reaction speeds compared to unisensory conditions, independent of temporal order.
However, a key dissociation emerged between unisensory modalities: while participants reacted significantly faster to visual stimuli, they achieved higher perceptual accuracy with touch.
Furthermore, although reaction times correlated with general presence scores, participants retrospectively rated touch as feeling significantly more "real" than vision.
These findings suggest a disconnect between the immediate, action-oriented "felt" presence dominated by vision and a reflective "judged" presence where touch is dominant.
By validating these effects using contact-free haptics, this research offers a new insight into how measures of presence are collected in virtual reality studies.

Fixed Effects Estimates for Linear Mixed-Effects Model Predicting Perceptual Sensitivity (d') From Unisensory ModalityThe fixed effects estimates, standard errors, t-values, and p-values for a linear mixedeffects model predicting d' from unisensory vision and unisensory touch scenarios.
The model includes random intercepts for ID, and BART score, SART score, Touch score, Vision score, Age, VR familiarity and VR touch familiarity as control variables.
Unisensory vision conditions exhibited a significantly reduced average d' than unisensory touch conditions.
